name: Armpit shaving

image.caption: After armpit shaving has left my skin upset and in agony for a third time in a row - I'm thinking of ditching it. I'll trim, but screw shaving. #feministandproud #bodyhairdontcare

lead: Shaving the underarms gives a smooth, groomed look right away, and some people do it hoping for less odor, reasoning that hair gives sweat and bacteria more surface to cling to.

A razor cuts the hair at the skin surface and regrowth takes days. Odor itself arises when bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus break down apocrine sweat. A 2012 study cited on Wikipedia reported that shaved and unshaved armpits were rated as smelling the same.

paras: Most people shave with a razor in the shower with shaving cream or gel, repeating every few days. It is often paired with deodorant or antiperspirant.
Razor irritation and nicks are common. Damaged skin may absorb more deodorant chemicals, and shared unsterilised barber tools have been linked to hepatitis C transmission in Pakistan.

Where Has All The Hair Gone?

chain: Less surface for sweat and bacteria
angle.text: Shaving the underarms gives a smooth, groomed look immediately, and is proposed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to cut odor held by hair. One study found shaved and unshaved armpits rated as smelling the same.

lead: Armpit shaving is the removal of underarm hair at the skin surface with a razor. It is the most common form of hair removal in general, and its results last only hours to days.[1] In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions it is proposed as a way to reduce body odor, on the reasoning that hair gives bacteria and sweat more surface to cling to.

Body odor in the armpit arises mainly when skin bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands.[2] One study cited on Wikipedia's underarm hair page reported that shaved and unshaved armpits were rated as smelling the same.[3] Published evidence on the topic is limited.

paras: Shaving cuts hair at the skin surface rather than removing the follicle, so regrowth is quick.[1] Underarm hair removal by shaving or other methods is common in some cultures, particularly among women.[3] Wikipedia's hair removal article notes that Harper's Bazaar ran a 1915 campaign presenting underarm hair removal as a necessity for women, and that a razor marketed to women followed shortly after.[1]

Wikipedia's hair removal article says hair can collect odor-causing microorganisms and that its removal has sometimes been used to reduce odor.[1] The body odor article describes armpit hair as helping to spread odors, while not discussing shaving.[2] The underarm hair article describes the exact function of the hair as unclear, and says some people claim it traps odor, a statement it presents without a citation.[3]

A 2017 study cited on the underarm hair page reported that shaving damaged skin increased absorption of deodorant chemicals from about 0.01 percent to 0.06 percent.[3] A 2003 study tentatively linked underarm shaving combined with antiperspirant use to earlier breast cancer diagnosis, but later studies reported no significant increase in breast cancer among users.[3]

In Pakistan, researchers have reported that many hepatitis C patients have a history of facial or armpit shaving at barber shops, and a 2011 laboratory study examined potash alum stones used on shaving cuts as a possible route of virus transmission.[4] This concerns shared, unsterilised barber equipment rather than personal razors.

No randomized trials of armpit shaving for body odor were found. A 2012 study cited on the underarm hair page reported that shaved and unshaved armpits were rated as smelling the same.[3] A separate line of research on barber-shop shaving and hepatitis C transmission is epidemiological and concerns infection risk, not odor.[4]
